--- title: "Shinylive: Serverless Shiny in the Browser" subtitle: "What it is, how it works, and when to use it" author: "Shayah LaCour" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-title: "Contents" code-fold: false execute: echo: true eval: false warning: false --- ```{=html}

🌐 Shinylive: Shiny Without a Server

How WebAssembly makes it possible to run R in your browser — and why that changes everything

``` ## The Traditional Problem Every Shiny app you've built so far has a fundamental constraint: **it needs a live R process running somewhere**. When a user moves a slider, their browser sends a message to that R process, R re-runs the relevant code, and the result travels back. The browser is just a display terminal. This is powerful — it means the full power of R and all its packages is available — but it creates friction: - You need a server (your own laptop, shinyapps.io, Posit Connect...) - Someone has to pay for that server - The app goes offline if the server does - Sharing becomes a deployment problem, not just a files problem **Shinylive solves this by making the server disappear entirely.** --- ## What is Shinylive? Shinylive is a version of Shiny that runs **entirely inside the user's web browser** using **WebAssembly (Wasm)**. There is no R server. R itself — the interpreter, the packages, everything — runs locally in the browser using a technology called [webR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/). ::: {.callout-note} ## WebAssembly in plain language WebAssembly is a low-level binary format that modern browsers can execute at near-native speed. Originally designed for C and C++ programs, it has been extended to run other languages — including R. The R interpreter has been compiled to Wasm and is distributed as a downloadable bundle. When a Shinylive app loads in your browser, it downloads that R bundle and starts executing your app code directly. ::: The result: a Shiny app that lives as a collection of static files (HTML, CSS, JS, Wasm blobs). You can host it on GitHub Pages, Netlify, any CDN — anywhere that can serve static files. No R process, no server management. --- ## How Shinylive Works Architecturally Here is a side-by-side comparison of the two architectures: ### Traditional Shiny ``` User browser ──── HTTP request ────► R Server ◄── rendered output ─── (Shiny running in R process) (input → reactive graph → output) ``` The browser is a thin client. All computation happens server-side. ### Shinylive ``` User browser ──── loads static files ────► CDN / GitHub Pages / Netlify ◄──── HTML + JS + Wasm ────── (no R process exists) [Browser now contains webR + your app code] [input → reactive graph → output all happen locally] ``` The browser is the entire compute environment. The CDN just serves files. --- ## Setting Up Shinylive in Quarto You don't need to install a separate package to use Shinylive in a Quarto document — you use the `shinylive` Quarto extension. ### Step 1: Install the extension ```bash # Run in your terminal from your project folder quarto add quarto-ext/shinylive ``` This adds an `_extensions/` folder to your project. ### Step 2: Add the filter to your YAML ```yaml --- title: "My Shinylive Document" format: html filters: - shinylive --- ``` ### Step 3: Write a `{shinylive-r}` code block ````markdown ```{shinylive-r} #| standalone: true library(shiny) ui <- fluidPage( sliderInput("n", "Number", 1, 100, 50), textOutput("result") ) server <- function(input, output) { output$result <- renderText(paste("Value:", input$n)) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` ```` When Quarto renders this document, it packages the app code and the webR runtime together. The resulting HTML file is fully self-contained — the Shiny app runs when anyone opens it. --- ## A Realistic Shinylive Example Here is a more complete example of a Shinylive app embedded in a Quarto document. This could sit in one of your dashboard or report pages and work for any reader without any server: ````markdown ```{shinylive-r} #| standalone: true #| viewerHeight: 500 library(shiny) library(ggplot2) channels <- c("Mobile", "Paid Search", "Affiliate", "Social Media") attr_df <- data.frame( channel = rep(channels, 3), model = rep(c("First Touch", "Last Touch", "Markov"), each = 4), credits = c(21, 34, 17, 10, 26, 15, 18, 8, 21, 20, 20, 21) ) ui <- fluidPage( titlePanel("Interactive Attribution Explorer"), sidebarLayout( sidebarPanel( checkboxGroupInput("models", "Show models:", choices = unique(attr_df$model), selected = unique(attr_df$model)) ), mainPanel(plotOutput("p")) ) ) server <- function(input, output) { output$p <- renderPlot({ sub <- attr_df[attr_df$model %in% input$models, ] ggplot(sub, aes(channel, credits, fill = model)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Credits", fill = NULL) }) } shinyApp(ui, server) ``` ```` ::: {.callout-tip} ## The `standalone: true` option This tells Shinylive that the code block contains a complete, self-contained app (with its own `shinyApp()` call), rather than just a fragment. Always include this for full apps. ::: --- ## Shinylive vs Traditional Shiny: Full Comparison ```{=html}
Dimension Traditional Shiny Shinylive
Where R runsServer (your machine, shinyapps.io, Posit Connect)User's browser (via WebAssembly)
Hosting requirementLive R process requiredAny static file host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, CDN)
Cost to hostFree tier limited; paid plans for scaleFree (static hosting is cheap or free)
Initial load timeFast (server already has R)Slower — browser must download webR runtime (~5–20 MB)
Computation speedFast (server-grade hardware)Slower (WebAssembly has overhead vs native)
Data privacyData sent to server (must secure server)Data never leaves the browser ✓
Package supportAny CRAN packageOnly packages compiled for Wasm (growing list)
Database connectionsFull support (server can connect to any DB)Not supported (no network sockets in Wasm)
File system accessFull server file systemSandboxed virtual file system only
ScalingRequires server scaling / load balancingInfinite scale (each user runs their own instance)
Offline useNo (requires server connection)Possible after initial load (assets can be cached)
Best forProduction apps, large data, DB connectionsEducational content, portfolios, reports, prototypes
``` --- ## Strengths of Shinylive ### 1. Zero infrastructure cost Because Shinylive apps are static files, you can host them on **GitHub Pages for free**. There is no shinyapps.io monthly plan, no Posit Connect license, no server to maintain. For a student portfolio or teaching materials, this is a significant advantage. ### 2. Perfect for embedding in Quarto documents Shinylive is deeply integrated with Quarto. A single `.qmd` file can contain text, code, plots, and live interactive Shiny widgets — all rendering to a single static HTML file. This makes it ideal for lecture notes, tutorials, and reproducible reports that need interactivity. ### 3. Data privacy by design Because all computation happens locally in the browser, sensitive data never travels across the network to a server. For healthcare, government, or financial applications where data privacy is paramount, this is a structural advantage. ### 4. Infinite scale Every user runs their own isolated R instance in their own browser tab. There is no shared server, so ten users or ten thousand users make no difference to the host. --- ## Weaknesses of Shinylive ### 1. Slow initial load The first time a user opens a Shinylive app, their browser must download the webR runtime — roughly 5–20 MB depending on which packages are needed. On a fast connection this takes a few seconds; on a slow one it can feel sluggish. Traditional Shiny apps load almost instantly because R is already running on the server. ### 2. Limited package support Not every R package can run in WebAssembly. Packages that depend on compiled C or Fortran code need to be specifically recompiled for Wasm. Posit maintains a growing list of supported packages, and popular ones like `ggplot2`, `dplyr`, and `tidyr` work — but if your app depends on a niche package, it may not be available yet. ### 3. No server-side resources Traditional Shiny can connect to databases, read large files from disk, call external APIs, or run long-running background jobs. Shinylive can't do any of this — WebAssembly runs in a sandboxed environment without access to network sockets or the host file system. ### 4. Slower computation WebAssembly executes at roughly 50–80% of native speed for CPU-bound work. For simple interactive dashboards this is imperceptible, but for computationally heavy tasks (large matrix operations, bootstrap simulations, complex model fitting), the overhead becomes noticeable. --- ## When to Choose Which ::: {.callout-tip} ## Quick decision guide **Choose Shinylive when:** - You're embedding interactivity in a Quarto report or teaching document - You want to host on GitHub Pages or Netlify for free - Your app uses common packages (ggplot2, dplyr, shiny) - Data is small and privacy matters - You want to share with anyone, no logins **Choose Traditional Shiny when:** - Your app connects to a database or reads large files - You need packages not yet available in webR - Your computation is heavy (fitting models, large data transformations) - You need production-grade uptime and monitoring - Your organization already has Posit Connect ::: --- ## The Bigger Picture: WebAssembly in Data Science Shinylive is part of a broader trend: moving data science tools to the browser using WebAssembly. **Pyodide** brings Python to the browser the same way webR does for R. Observable's **Observable Plot** and **DuckDB-Wasm** let you query millions of rows of data entirely client-side. The trajectory is clear: increasingly, analytical work that once required a server will be executable locally. This changes how we think about sharing analyses — instead of spinning up infrastructure, we publish a URL. For now, Shinylive sits at the intersection of these two worlds: it lowers the barrier to sharing interactive R work dramatically, at the cost of some performance and package coverage. As webR matures and more packages get compiled for Wasm, those limitations will shrink. --- ## Summary | | Traditional Shiny | Shinylive | |---|---|---| | **Core idea** | R on a server, browser as display | R in the browser via WebAssembly | | **Best use case** | Production apps, big data, DB | Portfolios, teaching, reports | | **Hosting** | Needs live R process | Any static host | | **Packages** | All of CRAN | Wasm-compiled subset | | **Privacy** | Data goes to server | Data stays in browser | Shinylive is not a replacement for traditional Shiny — it's a complement. Together, they cover the full spectrum from quick embeddable widgets to production enterprise applications, all within the same familiar R and Shiny programming model. --- ## References - Posit. *Shinylive: Shiny for Python and R, running in the browser.* https://shiny.posit.co/py/docs/shinylive.html - Chang, W. & Wickham, H. *Mastering Shiny.* O'Reilly, 2021. https://mastering-shiny.org - Allaire, J.J. et al. *Quarto documentation.* https://quarto.org/docs/interactive/shiny/ - webR project. *webR: R in the Browser.* https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/ - Mozilla Developer Network. *WebAssembly.* https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly
